issues.claim: Current paper and supporting evidence are in a single unambiguous, reviewable snapshot.
issues.evidence: `main` and `revision/adam-collapse-drift` point to f9f4b443; the latest branch points to 1064d67 and contains 201 additional blobs plus 100 modified paths. The latest branch has a corrected theorem, progress ledger, paper-assets checker, T01/T02/T03, readout report, E32 and pending K14/K15 artifacts. These aren't on the default branch.
issues.impact: A reviewer cloning default `main` would read a different paper/evidence state and miss important fixes and limitations. There is no PR to define the canonical merge boundary.
issues.author_counterargument: The claude branch is the active working branch and main is simply behind.
issues.resolution: Before submission, nominate one canonical commit and merge or tag it; archive older drafts; regenerate all tables and ledgers at that commit.

issues.claim: The corrected bound provides a novel optimizer-independent result explaining collapse.
issues.evidence: The norm inequality follows from `||mean(w_k)|| ≤ mean||w_k||`; with observed holders' mean gain Gbar and non-holder loss Dbar, contraction follows if pGbar−(1−p)Dbar<0. Correct but conditional on observed updates. It is not a predictive optimization theorem by itself; T01's 0/1,200 violations check this inequality, which is a triangle-inequality bound.
issues.impact: The theorem can support a diagnostic framing, but novelty/significance must come from the empirically measured optimizer–aggregation mechanism and useful fix, not the generic inequality alone.
issues.author_counterargument: The threshold θ is informative when measured G/D are tied to optimizer and long-tail data; the work is explicit that the bound itself is optimizer-free.
issues.resolution: Call it a conditional contraction bound; separate (i) tautological bound validity, (ii) measured G/D mechanism, and (iii) empirical collapse. Don't use zero bound violations as independent evidence for Adam behavior.

issues.claim: Any nonzero coupled Adam weight-decay coefficient produces an approximately λ-independent full learning-rate-sized row shrink over all relevant non-holder updates.
issues.evidence: The draft now qualifies the argument by λ|w_j|≫ε and acknowledges sparse-gradient steps can exceed η. In code, each client has persistent Adam optimizer state across rounds while global parameters are reset to aggregated weights. T01 tests one MNIST split/seed (40 rounds) and sees λ=1e−4 and 1e−3 similarly collapse, and wd=0 does not; it is not an unrestricted theorem over persistent state, zero crossings, ε-dominated rows, or other architectures.
issues.impact: The empirical mechanism is plausible and supported, but any universal optimizer statement or transfer to DCGAN/DDPM/FedAvg variants is overstated. T02 shows dilution even without decay.
issues.author_counterargument: The paper narrows it to the regime actually measured, reports λ-invariance empirically, and separates dilution from decay.
issues.resolution: State the per-coordinate assumptions and optimizer-state conditions; report T01 as one-seed mechanism evidence. Run K15's matched AdamW/no-decay/lazy-decay comparisons before claiming HWA is the best fix.

issues.location: Claude `docs/PROGRESS.md` §3; K15 specs and NB38/NB39; tables T17/T18
issues.claim: The proposed HWA/ESA treatment is superior to simpler optimizer fixes for conditioning-row collapse.
issues.evidence: K15 explicitly schedules matched AdamW (wd=1e−3), AdamW 1e−2 at K=10, no weight decay on class rows, lazy decay, compared against HWA. `docs/PROGRESS.md` says notebooks ready, not run; tables T17/T18 have 20 missing cells each.
issues.impact: This is the most direct alternative explanation for the optimizer-related contribution. Without it, the paper cannot claim HWA is superior to simply correcting the decay implementation or removing decay from the conditioning rows.
issues.author_counterargument: K15 is planned and can be added in a revision; HWA may still win because it fixes dilution as well as shrinkage.
issues.resolution: Run K15 at K=10/50/100 with same splits/seeds and matched generator/optimizer budgets. At minimum compare row norms, tail fidelity, balanced accuracy, and runtime. Until then, narrow claims to demonstrated alternatives.

issues.claim: The algorithm automatically chooses mean anchoring vs class-row/HWA fallback from statistic F at runtime.
issues.evidence: The core computes/logs F from class statistics, but `stage_ii` chooses behavior based on configured `m['gen']['type']`; no `if F < 0.05` branch controls generator type there. The report describes an automatic separation gate; the experiment results are run using preselected variants/configs.
issues.impact: The claimed data-dependent switch is not demonstrated by the executable current pipeline as one adaptive algorithm. This is a reproducibility and algorithm-description issue, not proof that the reported per-dataset results are false.
issues.author_counterargument: Separate predeclared configurations were used for datasets, and F is a no-test-label statistic that explains which branch to run.
issues.resolution: Implement a genuine runtime switch driven only by released training statistics, test it on unseen/intermediate-F data, or describe the reported numbers as a manually configured per-dataset variant rather than an automatic method.

issues.claim: The implemented transform gives exactly the real class mean and spread and is minimum-displacement optimal.
issues.evidence: The raw affine scalar map is optimal for unconstrained maps matching mean and total second central moment under its stated assumptions. Implementation clips scale to [0.1,10] and applies `ReLU` after the affine transform. ReLU changes means and covariance/spread; clipping can prevent reaching the target at all. Empirical spread approaches but is not exactly 1.
issues.impact: The mathematical optimum can hold for the ideal affine map, not the implemented clipped/ReLU transform. Claims should say approximate/statistics-targeted after projection, backed by residual measurements.
issues.author_counterargument: FE features are non-negative and projection is necessary; empirical spread ratios are close to real spread.
issues.resolution: State theorem for the unconstrained affine map, then characterize the projected map separately. Log pre/post-ReLU moment errors and failure cases for all classes/seeds.

issues.claim: MC-S/MC-B corrects exact class covariance by the minimum-displacement Gelbrich map.
issues.evidence: Covariance path uses only top-k (k≤256) subspace, shrinks small-sample class covariances toward pooled or generator covariance, clips eigenvalues of A to [0.1,10], scales orthogonal residual by a scalar, and then applies ReLU. Therefore it cannot generally match the full empirical class covariance exactly nor achieve unconstrained global minimum displacement after these operations.
issues.impact: The transport derivation may justify a core subspace map before stabilizers, but not all implemented approximations as one exact global optimum. This matters most for the new MC-S/MC-B claim and high-dimensional datasets.
issues.author_counterargument: The paper distinguishes subspace covariance from total spread and regularizes tails to reduce estimator variance; MC-B results are encouraging.
issues.resolution: Rename guarantee to regularized/subspace approximation; report covariance residuals after clipping/ReLU; prove any narrower guarantee for the composed map; clearly mark MC-B as provisional pending five-seed comparison.

issues.claim: Herding to the exact kernel embedding lowers the classification-risk term for arbitrary downstream heads.
issues.evidence: Implementation uses 6,144 random Fourier features, so the target is a finite random-feature approximation, not the exact infinite-dimensional RKHS embedding. Greedy candidate selection reduces discrepancy for the finite feature map, conditional on the candidate pool. The displayed bound requires loss in a bounded RKHS ball; the manuscript does not establish that the deep heterogeneous heads' relevant losses satisfy this assumption.
issues.impact: The finite-RFF matching is an implementable heuristic with empirical support, but the general risk-bound interpretation is conditional and may not apply to these neural classifiers.
issues.author_counterargument: The authors use a standard MMD/RKHS result and explicitly treat the head loss as a condition of the lemma.
issues.resolution: Make the bound explicitly conditional, do not claim the neural risk is guaranteed to improve without an RKHS-norm assumption, and measure approximation/convergence sensitivity to RFF dimension and pool factor.

issues.claim: A scalar estimator result explains why 10 synthetic epochs should improve neural classifier accuracy after anchoring.
issues.evidence: Proposition uses an assumed MSE formula with unbiased real samples, equal per-sample variance, synthetic label bias b, and a scalar mixing-weight estimator. Neural SGD on correlated generated features, soft labels, repeated epochs, nonconvex heads, and client-specific distributions do not directly satisfy this model. The experiments do show extra fake epochs help MNIST/FashionMNIST more than low-fidelity CIFAR/SVHN and hurt final-round accuracy in hard settings.
issues.impact: Useful qualitative intuition but not a theorem about neural optimization or an optimal epoch count. Overstated causal/explanatory language weakens theory novelty.
issues.author_counterargument: The paper describes a stylized model and reports its converse on low-fidelity datasets.
issues.resolution: Call it a toy bias-variance model; articulate mapping assumptions; present empirical interaction rather than claiming derivation of T_s=10 for neural training.

issues.claim: Exact class statistics, class prototype anchoring, feature generation, classifier recalibration and long-tail FL provide sufficient novelty over prior art.
issues.evidence: Building blocks are established: prototype transfer (FedProto), class-conditional data-free heterogeneous FL (FedGen/FedFTG/DENSE/FedCG/GeFL), class calibration/retraining (CCVR, CReFF, Fed3R), logit adjustment/FedLC, MMD/kernel herding, Gelbrich covariance mapping, and class-wise aggregation in FL/recommendation. The strongest novelty appears to be the coupled-Adam/FedAvg failure analysis in the GeFL-F generator and putting multiple aggregate statistics to work in a heterogeneous-generator pipeline; the review should not dismiss that combination as inherently non-novel.
issues.impact: Novelty hinges on specific evidence of incremental value over simpler HWA+LA+CSL and direct recalibration/statistics-based methods; broad claims of novel building blocks won't hold.
issues.author_counterargument: Paper openly attributes each component to prior sources and claims novelty in integration and setting.
issues.resolution: Add method-by-method comparison with CReFF/CCVR/Fed3R and closest prototype/statistics transfer; claim novelty of measured failure mechanism + integrated anchoring only where directly supported.

issues.claim: The large Ours-A gain over GeFL-F reflects a large incremental contribution beyond existing classifier-side fixes.
issues.evidence: New readout report shows GeFL-F final heads gain from pooled-real last-layer refit/oracle by +16.5 MNIST, +20.5 FMNIST, +14.3 SVHN points. Approximate oracle baseline levels are 90.7/79.2/64.8 versus Ours-A 94.8/79.7/65.6, margins only +4.1/+0.5/+0.8. With readout/refit applied to both methods Ours-A oracle margins +4.2/+2.4/+3.6. This oracle has pooled real training access and is not a fair deployable federated baseline, but it quantifies how much of the apparent gap is readout error.
issues.impact: Headline gains over uncorrected GeFL-F are not incremental gains over the strongest relevant classifier recalibration family. FashionMNIST/SVHN margin may be within noise.
issues.author_counterargument: The oracle is centralized/upper-bound, the paper itself says recalibration baseline must be included, and a federated exact-readout path is now tested on a reduced schedule.
issues.resolution: Implement matched CReFF/CCVR/Fed3R-style baselines under the same frozen FE, head architecture, long-tail partitions and training budgets. If using ER-LDA, run full schedule/multi-seed and compare both methods with ER.

issues.location: Claude `docs/PROGRESS.md` §§1,3; K14/K15 specs and T17/T18 tables
issues.claim: The current evidence is complete enough to substantiate all major claims.
issues.evidence: K14 (ablation seeds 3–4, MC-B validation) and K15 (AdamW/no-decay/lazy decay comparisons at K=10/50/100) are marked ready but not run. The corresponding branch has notebooks and generated tables, but 20 missing cells in T17 and 20 in T18; K09 per-component significance is still weak at n=3.

issues.author_counterargument: K14/K15 are prepared jobs and can be completed later; the one-seed theory test is mathematically valid.

issues.claim: Thirty negative component-removal comparisons establish an aggregate sign-test p=2e−9.
issues.evidence: The 30 differences come from 5 component removals x 2 datasets x 3 seeds, and reuse the same full-model seed runs, partitions and generated artifacts. They are correlated comparisons, not 30 independent replicates. The current branch analysis correctly says no single component remains significant after Holm correction over 10 tests at n=3 (smallest adjusted p=.085); small MC/KH/FashionMNIST-PC effects are weak.
issues.impact: Aggregate p-value massively overstates evidence if treated as independent sample count. Per-component evidence must be reported with its correct unit and multiplicity.
issues.author_counterargument: All paired differences were directionally negative; the analysis itself qualifies per-component significance and says K14 is pending.
issues.resolution: Remove the global 30-pair sign-test as confirmatory evidence; report paired effects per component/dataset with uncertainty and Holm-adjusted p-values; run seeds 3–4.

issues.location: `Tracker.update` in `experiments/core.py`; `best_mean_acc` columns and paper IID tables
issues.claim: All headline metrics are equally fair because the same metrics are used for every method.
issues.evidence: The tracker updates the best score as max over each architecture's test accuracy every evaluated round; `best_mean_acc` therefore selects the best round using test labels/metrics. PROGRESS says the paper's balanced-setting comparisons retain this metric to match the original paper, while long-tail headlines use `final_bal`. Equal leakage across methods does not make a held-out test set valid for model selection.
issues.impact: IID best-round gains are optimistic and should not be the sole evidence for generalization. It makes cross-setting tables mix different estimands if not labeled prominently.
issues.author_counterargument: The comparison intentionally reproduces GeFL-F's original reported protocol; long-tail headline uses final checkpoints.
issues.resolution: Keep protocol-reproduction table labeled as historical comparison; add validation-selected checkpoints or final-round results for all methods on the same seeds. Never tune on the test set for the paper's final main table.

issues.claim: Every quoted paper number matches its generated table and raw per-seed results.
issues.evidence: CHECK.md enumerates draft-vs-data discrepancies, including IID MNIST 96.02 vs 96.01; K=100 MNIST client rows; E16 long-tail balanced/tail numbers; T_s=10 values; CIFAR-10 CSL 60.02 vs 59.85; DDPM-F 83.10 vs 82.82. issues.location: Main tables, T01, T03, E31/E32, K09/K14
issues.claim: The reported small improvements are robust across randomness.
issues.evidence: Many headline runs n=3; T01 is n=1; T03/T03b are n=1 on reduced schedule; K01 CIFAR-10 paired JSONL is missing so its p-values are Welch/unpaired; MC-B has one MNIST LT seed at 92.50 vs ~95.9 others and remains pending extra seeds. Some gains are only 0.3–1 points (FMNIST baseline recalibration and ablation components).
issues.impact: Large MNIST LT gains look consistent, but small increments and mechanism claims lack strong uncertainty resolution; overprecision/significance claims should be softened.
issues.author_counterargument: Three matched seeds are normal for preliminary work and the branch labels weak evidence/pending status transparently.
issues.resolution: Run planned seeds and publish mean±SD plus paired differences and CIs; distinguish high-powered effects from descriptive direction-only evidence.

issues.location: `experiments/core.py` clipping calibration in `run_one`; E26 spec/results; paper §4.7
issues.claim: The reported epsilon/delta-DP statistic release is independent of private-data calibration choices and applies as stated.
issues.evidence: E26 claims a public clipping bound, but the simulation estimates it as the 90th-percentile feature norm from `ctx.part['heldout']`, built by taking 200 training-corpus examples per class out of the benchmark training split and not assigning them to a simulated client. For the benchmark corpus these may be publicly known data, but that is an explicit dataset/public-pool assumption, not an automatic deployment property. DP guarantee is conditional on treating this bound/pool as public or outside protected client records.
issues.impact: Potential privacy-accounting circularity if the bound derives from data included in the privacy unit. This is not by itself proof the benchmark E26 result violates DP because the held-out subset is disjoint from client partitions and the datasets are public; applicability to real private client records is not established.
issues.author_counterargument: The split holds the calibration pool out from all clients and uses a public benchmark; nothing from those samples is uploaded by a client.
issues.resolution: Precisely specify adjacency and protected records; provide a truly public/external calibration pool or fixed data-independent norm bound; document whether the held-out sample belongs to the DP domain.

issues.claim: ESA as a full FL protocol is differentially private.
issues.evidence: The manuscript correctly states the generator's own FedAvg is not DP and describes DP on the additional anchoring statistic releases only; the formal evaluation covers MNIST/FMNIST K=10 scalar MC route at ε∈{8,2}, δ=1e−5. Other model-training updates, frozen FE process, local client heads, and standard GeFL-F generator messages are not covered by this guarantee.
issues.impact: Acceptable as a scoped claim if strictly written as DP for additional aggregate statistics, but fatal to any reading of “the full training process is DP.” Privacy-utility generalization to covariance gate and SVHN not tested.
issues.author_counterargument: Limitations explicitly disclose generator FedAvg is not DP; paper says 'every released anchoring statistic' can be privatized, not full protocol.
issues.resolution: Title/table/callout should consistently say “DP of the added anchoring-statistic releases”; map every release and budget. Do not claim end-to-end DP. Run/correct MC-S/MC-B privacy scope only if claimed.

issues.claim: The DP evaluation validates all ESA variants, including covariance correction.
issues.evidence: When `_STAT_DP` is active, `run_one` bypasses `CovCalibratedGen`/MC-S and falls back to `MomentCalibratedGen` for a requested covariance route. DP raw statistics for pooled dense covariance and class subspace covariance matrices are not covered by E26's reported MNIST/FMNIST scalar-anchor experiment. E26 is useful evidence only for its configured releases/variant.
issues.impact: Do not generalize scalar-MC DP results to MC-S/MC-B or covariance anchoring; covariance route needs its own clipping sensitivity, noise, and zCDP accounting.
issues.author_counterargument: MC-S privacy is not claimed in E26; the final DP table is the scalar MC configuration.
issues.resolution: State exact DP-enabled configuration in table and add tests only if DP MC-S/MC-B is claimed. Ensure every released covariance, PCA basis, and gate input is included in sensitivity/compose accounting.

issues.claim: The evaluated implementation operationally uses secure aggregation so that the server sees only sums.
issues.evidence: The simulator constructs `X = torch.cat(feats)`/`Y = torch.cat(ys_list)` and centrally forms counts/sums/covariances; the research protocol describes those sums as secure-aggregated messages, but the experiment code does not execute cryptographic secure aggregation. Secure aggregation is a system assumption/protocol design, not something tested by this simulator.
issues.impact: The algorithm could be implemented atop secure aggregation, but runtime/performance evidence does not validate the cryptographic protocol, fault/dropout behavior, or server-observation model.
issues.author_counterargument: The work is algorithm research; Bonawitz-style aggregation is specified as the communication primitive and not meant to implement crypto in the research simulator.
issues.resolution: Say “simulated centrally; protocol sends secure-aggregated sums in deployment.” Explicitly state server trust, thresholds, collusion assumptions, client dropout and per-message protected fields.
issues.status: Needs clarity, not an algorithm fatality

issues.claim: The added communication remains about 0.3 MB apart from the small class-level terms for the main method/covariance option.
issues.evidence: Mean/spread/RFF upload is about 69,000 numbers for D=768 and C=10. Covariance mode also computes a dense pooled D×D sum and class subspace moments C×k×k (k=256), plus class projected first/second moments. A D×D float matrix is about 4.7MB at D=768 or 26.2MB at D=2560 using float32 (about twice with float64), before per-class k×k matrices and protocol overhead. “0.3MB” applies to mean/spread/RFF path only.
issues.impact: Covariance variant has materially different client upload, server memory and latency. Headline cost is underestimation if read as applying to all ESA variants.
issues.author_counterargument: The paper separately says “plus Ck² numbers when covariance is used”; dense M can perhaps be streamed or represented in a lower precision in a real protocol.
issues.resolution: Give per-variant bytes per client/server, dtypes, number of rounds and whether covariance sums are split/streamed; report measured peak memory and latency for SVHN/CIFAR dimensions.

issues.location: Paper privacy section / statistics list; secure-aggregation assumptions
issues.claim: Secure aggregate totals reveal nothing except safe federation-wide facts.
issues.evidence: Secure aggregation hides individual client messages from the server under assumptions, but global class counts, mean/covariance/RFF totals can expose rare class support or sensitive population properties, and single-client classes can be inferred at federation level. The handout recognizes single-client class disclosure; blanket wording “reveal nothing beyond federation-level totals” is technically tautological not a privacy guarantee.
issues.impact: Privacy characterization must distinguish secure aggregation from differential privacy and describe what global statistics reveal.
issues.author_counterargument: The DP mechanism provides a utility/privacy trade-off for these stats and secure aggregation is not claimed to hide the released global sum.
issues.resolution: Narrow language to “server sees only the aggregate under secure aggregation”; quantify membership/attribute risks for rare classes and make DP the guarantee for these releases.

issues.claim: Between/within ratio F with threshold 0.05 indicates when class means do not carry class identity.
issues.evidence: Reported F≈0.01 for SVHN, ≈0.14–0.60 in other datasets. The bound limits generated-class W1 separation under Lipschitz assumptions; it does not prove F<0.05 is a universally valid cutoff. The threshold is chosen after examining four datasets and is not validated on an intermediate-F or unseen dataset.
issues.impact: The separation diagnostic is useful, but the fixed threshold and automatic-selection claim may overfit these datasets; it needs a sensitivity/generalization test.
issues.author_counterargument: The paper discloses that the rule is set from four datasets and explicitly calls for intermediate separation to be tested.
issues.resolution: Add a preregistered threshold sweep or held-out dataset with intermediate F, compare mean, covariance, and HWA row routes, and describe threshold as heuristic until then.
issues.status: Known limitation acknowledged; key experiment missing

issues.claim: Headline results represent one consistent deployed method and metric.
issues.evidence: The code returns `final_bal` on trained heads, then computes `bbc_bal` as an additional calibrated-head metric; `balanced_bias_calibration` builds bias wrappers for evaluation and `bbc_applied` is recorded separately. Some prose cites raw values, some cites calibrated values (e.g., CIFAR 46.1 vs ~49). Tables mix final-round balanced accuracy for LT with `best_mean_acc` for IID reproduction. The output model/calibration setting must be exactly stated.
issues.impact: Different metrics answer different questions; comparisons become ambiguous if GeFL-F and ESA or cross-setting values use different calibration/model-selection rules.
issues.author_counterargument: Paper reports calibration as a separate metric and explains the original-paper best-round protocol.
issues.resolution: Choose one primary metric per table, label raw vs BBC outputs, apply the same inference procedure to all methods where applicable, and export reproducible calibration offsets/models. Keep IID historical replication table separate.

issues.claim: ESA is broadly robust across heterogeneous federated learning and long-tail settings.
issues.evidence: Primary evaluations are four image benchmarks using a shared frozen feature extractor and GeFL-F's ten-head architecture framework, long-tail IF=100/Dirichlet(0.5), balanced IID settings and some client counts. Hard-dataset and new covariance variants have fewer runs in some conditions. No non-image, changing-client, temporal drift, partial participation or unseen-feature-space result is present.
issues.impact: Claim should be scoped to this protocol. It does not establish broad FL robustness or transfer to changing clients/feature spaces.
issues.author_counterargument: Paper explicitly keeps the frozen FE and reference GeFL-F protocol to isolate this contribution and discloses the limitation.
issues.resolution: Use exact scope wording, add one held-out dataset/protocol only if making broad claims, and do not extrapolate from K=100 MNIST to every large federation.

issues.claim: All reported experimental results are reproducible from checked-in raw per-seed results.
issues.evidence: Claude branch materially improves traceability and says LEDGER covers 1,177 runs, but PROGRESS says K01 CIFAR-10 raw `runs.jsonl` was never copied back (summary only), K09 `runs.csv` omits `-PC` arms due to worker overwrite while JSONL and summary are complete, and K15/K14 raw results do not exist because runs are pending. This is a partial artifact gap, not broad absence of results.
issues.impact: Reproduce certain summary claims/tests remains difficult. Claims must be tied only to logged source data; no unsupported claim should be presumed false.
issues.author_counterargument: Raw JSONL is primary for most runs, and some results are summary-only due Kaggle transfer not because experiment never ran.
issues.resolution: Recover K01 CIFAR run zip/logs if possible; regenerate CSV from merged JSONL; tag output files with source notebook/commit/job/seed; maintain branch-specific ledger.
issues.status: Partially resolved on latest branch; still open

issues.claim: Every ESA component makes a statistically confirmed contribution to the final method.
issues.evidence: K09 runs n=3; effects small for MC/KH and PC on FMNIST; corrected analysis says no single arm survives Holm adjustment over 10 tests (minimum adjusted p .085). All paired changes are negative, which is directional evidence, not componentwise significance. K14 is pending.
issues.impact: Need avoid implying each component is independently established, especially for minor effects. The ablation is still valuable in showing consistent direction and effect heterogeneity.
issues.author_counterargument: Updated branch accurately marks weak significance and proposes K14 for the next pass.
issues.resolution: Report unadjusted and Holm-adjusted values and effect sizes. Add seeds 3–4, and predefine the family of tests. Discuss LA/BBC redundancy.

issues.claim: MC-B is a reliable across-dataset improvement over MC/MC-S.
issues.evidence: FMNIST LT 81.57±0.31 vs prior Ours-A ~79.7 across 3 seeds, FMNIST IID `best_mean_acc` 85.75±0.45 vs paper's best 84.28. MNIST LT 94.76±1.95 includes seed 2 at 92.50, a 2.7-point loss vs the other seeds and previous method. Progress marks it promising, pending K14 seeds 3–4.
issues.impact: MC-B may be an important better covariance strategy but is not yet uniformly robust; choose carefully whether the headline final method includes it.
issues.author_counterargument: The branch presents it as promising and exposes the unstable MNIST seed.
issues.resolution: Run five-seed paired comparison, fix final-method selection without test-set tuning, report tail/worst-class accuracy as well as balanced accuracy, and state conditional benefits.

issues.claim: The proposed exact readout and explanation of residual bias are established under full training.
issues.evidence: ER-LDA is within 0.8 points of a pooled-real oracle in 9/9 rows but evidence here is one seed and 0.4 schedule on CPU. Original synthetic-mean mismatch hypothesis P3 failed; revised scale normalization recovered only 16–34% of readout gap. Source-label confounding is labelled leading hypothesis, not tested. Full-schedule 3-seed oracle gaps exist but do not themselves validate ER full schedule.
issues.impact: Exact readout is a potentially strong known-style baseline, but claims about mechanism/close-to-oracle federated correction need robust full-schedule evidence.
issues.author_counterargument: The report explicitly labels preregistration failures and open hypotheses and claims only preliminary validation.
issues.resolution: Run full schedule and seeds on MNIST/FMNIST/SVHN/CIFAR; compare ER-LDA against oracle, BBC and current heads; keep failed H-R hypothesis out of final causal narrative.

issues.claim: Conditional class collapse itself is new.
issues.evidence: The newer branch explicitly cites Collapse by Conditioning (ICLR 2022) and distinguishes that centralized limited-data mode-collapse mechanism from the federated non-holder coupled Adam decay + FedAvg mechanism; it also adds FedAwS/FedNCF context for class/item embeddings and sparse class updates. This resolves a much broader novelty objection from the earlier main-only audit.
issues.impact: The collapse phenomenon alone is not novel; the precise optimizer-plus-aggregation mechanism may be an original, useful diagnosis if fully supported. Literature framing on Claude is improved but still must compare mechanics, not simply say no one else observes collapse.
issues.author_counterargument: Latest branch explicitly says the novelty is the federated mechanism, not class-conditional collapse itself.
issues.resolution: Keep nuanced claim, cite primary sources accurately, compare update recurrences and experimental regimes, avoid novelty assertion from omission alone.

issues.claim: Combining known blocks is itself a strong enough NeurIPS novelty argument.
issues.evidence: Mean prototypes, scalar moments, Gelbrich map, random Fourier features/MMD, kernel herding, HWA, LA, consensus distillation and bias calibration are mostly established tools. The latest manuscript makes an effort to name sources and distinguish contributions, but the principled unification and measured setting-specific benefit require direct tests. CReFF overlaps directly with heterogeneous/long-tailed FL classifier recalibration.
issues.impact: A combination can be novel, but it must show why the anchoring principle is more than an engineering stack and which features uniquely contribute beyond strong/simple alternatives.
issues.author_counterargument: Paper explicitly says components exist and claims the novelty is exact-statistics anchoring throughout a generator-based heterogeneous FL pipeline.
issues.resolution: Emphasize single principle, identify what stats each stage uses and why the same secure aggregate serves each, and show an ablation/strong baseline comparison isolating anchor from HWA+LA+CSL/BBC/recalibration.

issues.claim: All evaluation choices use only federated training statistics and do not inspect test data.
issues.evidence: The code's `make_partition` constructs a held-out pool from the same public benchmark training corpus but excludes it from clients. The separation statistic F uses training class sums; `ncm_acc` is computed against `feats_te` and test labels but is diagnostic only, not part of the F threshold in current code. That diagnostic should not be described as server-computable or usable at inference.
issues.impact: The current metric is not automatically a leakage flaw if it is diagnostic only, but it can confuse readers about whether a deployment gate requires test labels. The calibration pool's public status also needs the assumption in PRIV-01.
issues.author_counterargument: Code comment says NCM is diagnostic only; the intended gate is F from train sums.
issues.resolution: Document that F alone is the gate statistic; keep `ncm_acc` in offline diagnosis only, do not mention it as server input or use it for thresholds.

issues.location: BatchNorm state averaging; handout limitation and code `Averager`
issues.claim: FedAvg of model state dicts faithfully averages client distributional state for all buffers.
issues.evidence: The handout and progress note acknowledge averaging BatchNorm running variances omits between-client variance. This is an implementation limitation especially with highly non-IID client features; the same architecture/head matching avoids averaging different head types, but BN buffer semantics still matter.
issues.impact: Potentially biases feature distributions and variance, partially confounding the exact-spread and model aggregation analysis. Likely moderate, not enough to discard main result without a control.
issues.author_counterargument: The limitation is disclosed and inherited from reference GeFL-F protocol, not unique to ESA.
issues.resolution: State this in limitations and add FedBN or pooled-moment running-stat control if the argument depends on accurate variance; use same protocol for baseline/final comparisons.

issues.location: MC-S/MC-B communication, server covariance construction, all experiments
issues.claim: Method is scalable to many clients with acceptable communication/latency based on K=100 accuracy results.
issues.evidence: K=100 results are MNIST-centered; the high-dimensional covariance route computes a dense pooled covariance and class-subspace matrices and uses a server-side eigendecomposition. No wall-clock / client memory / communication evaluation across all branches or asynchronous/partial participation. Accuracy at K=100 is not a full scalability measurement.
issues.impact: The paper can claim accuracy scales to K=100 in the tested setting, not that the complete protocol is system-scalable under broader use.
issues.author_counterargument: Methods run in T4 environments and supplement provides rough notebook times; systems engineering isn't the central contribution.
issues.resolution: Separate accuracy scaling from resource scaling; report measured time/memory/bytes for D=768 and D=2560 covariance cases, and limit deployment claims.

issues.claim: The full set of listed runs can be reliably recreated from the repository by rerunning scripts as is.
issues.evidence: Newest branch improves reproducibility with a run ledger and a generated paper-asset script. But notebooks require Kaggle GPU T4×2/internet in some cases, some source raw runs have not been copied back, some result artifacts are generated after the source scripts were modified, and model/dataset acquisition paths require setup. This is improved traceability, not turnkey full replication.
issues.impact: Reproducibility has improved significantly vs main but is not turnkey; reproducibility claims should identify hardware/data/checkpoints and exact commit.
issues.author_counterargument: The branch instructs to reconstruct assets and provides Kaggle notebooks/artifacts; infrastructure limitations are disclosed.
issues.resolution: Add environment lockfile, one-command local smoke test, immutable run config per JSONL, exact source commit per artifact, and a clean generation check in CI.

issues.location: Current full/short paper drafts, handout and report in different branch refs
issues.claim: The repository contains a submission-ready, anonymized NeurIPS manuscript.
issues.evidence: The branch includes markdown working drafts, HTML reports and Word/PDF handouts; it does not in the reviewed tree provide a final anonymized NeurIPS-formatted 9-content-page PDF+checklist as prescribed in the official handbook. Main branch is stale and `claude` carries noncanonical handout/editorial artifacts; code/figures have repository owner/branch metadata that must be anonymized if linked under double-blind review.
issues.impact: Even a correct research result is not submission-ready until converted into official format, kept anonymous and supported by a single consistent supplemental ZIP. Nine-content-page rule and other submission conditions matter.
issues.author_counterargument: The repository is an in-progress research project, not a final submission package.
issues.resolution: Create an anonymized submission branch/tag with final LaTeX/PDF, appendix, checklist and separate anonymized supplement; ensure citations/links and repo metadata do not reveal authors if required by review policy.

issues.claim: Balanced accuracy alone demonstrates rare-class robustness.
issues.evidence: Some MC-B/branch reports show improved mean/balanced accuracy while worst-class accuracy can be low: E32 FMNIST long-tail worst class 33.19±4.02 vs balanced accuracy81.57; seed 2 instability on MNIST LT. The notebook/progress mentions per-class tail metrics, but headlines often emphasize balanced accuracy and omit worst-class/recall variability.
issues.impact: A high average can hide catastrophic rare-class performance; this matters directly to the motivation that “rare classes come back.”
issues.author_counterargument: Tail and worst metrics are logged in raw summary artifacts; main results include tail recall.
issues.resolution: Report worst-class, mean tail recall and per-class recall distribution for final candidate, especially MC-B and SVHN, in same table and seed pairing.

issues.claim: The gate covers intermediate mean separability and chooses the best source of class identity in unseen settings.
issues.evidence: F values across the four datasets are well separated (SVHN≈0.01, others≈0.14–0.60); this gives no empirical evidence at F near the 0.05 cutoff. Covariance on FashionMNIST may improve IID but harms MNIST LT, MC-B varies by dataset/seed. The gate criterion does not compare measured class covariance informativeness online, only mean-separation F.
issues.impact: F could be a useful flag for a bad mean anchor, but low mean-separability does not by itself prove that covariance correction or HWA is the best route.
issues.author_counterargument: The authors acknowledge an intermediate-F dataset is future work and use F solely to detect an anchor limitation.
issues.resolution: Add held-out intermediate regime and evaluate candidate branches on non-test validation data; treat covariance route as heuristic and report selection error/cost.

issues.claim: Ensemble agreement is an unbiased or generally more reliable target for generated features.
issues.evidence: The authors test Bayesian CSL and report circularity: heads trained in related settings can agree due to shared generator errors; half-one-hot/half-ensemble is a useful empirical blend but not generally unbiased. E18 rejected Bayesian CSL; E16/F10 show CSL small effects and in IID sometimes gains sub-point. Claims should remain empirical and conditional on different head errors.
issues.impact: The label method is a known distillation technique in a new feature-transfer location, not a correctness guarantee about consensus labels.
issues.author_counterargument: Paper openly reports failed Bayesian variant and uses beta=.5 due to experiments.
issues.resolution: Avoid unbiased/“better label” universal claims; include error correlation/teacher diversity; report its modest effect with multiple comparisons.
issues.status: Mostly resolved by transparent negative results

issues.location: Claude `docs/paper_single_idea.md` §4.1; HWA aggregator and effective number weights
issues.claim: Effective-number weighting is the statistically optimal holder aggregation weighting in this setting.
issues.evidence: HWA weights holders by E(n)=(1−β^n)/(1−β), motivated by a saturating effective-sample-number/variance model; branch docs say counts and uniform-holder averages were ablated, but direct proof that this weight is inverse variance for learned row estimates is not established by current loss model. In main code, weights are computed from client counts and row state dict aggregate; client-specific data/optimizer histories may create correlated, biased row estimates.
issues.impact: HWA's empirical performance can stand without an optimality claim. Stronger claims about inverse-variance optimality require a model and variance measurement.
issues.author_counterargument: It is a known weighting heuristic adapted from effective number, and weighting is compared empirically.
issues.resolution: Present as motivated heuristic; compare uniform-holder and raw-count HWA under current full protocol; measure row estimation error by n_kc before claiming optimality.

issues.location: Claude Appendix B; E24 KME-Gen; K13 VCT
issues.claim: Discarded methods and negative experiments are adequately represented.
issues.evidence: Latest branch reports failures: KME-Gen beats GeFL-F but trails PC+MC; VCT is worse than MixUp on long-tail and slightly above feature MixUp IID but neither reaches image-space MixUp; Bayesian CSL, lazy decay with HWA and server distillation are discarded. This is a strength, although branch reports/tables still need to be synchronized.
issues.impact: This is positive evidence of research completeness and helps narrow the best contribution to a coherent anchored stack. It should not be scored as a weakness by itself.
issues.author_counterargument: The manuscript already lists these in Appendix B and PROGRESS marks VCT negative.
issues.resolution: Keep this candor; ensure paper assets include the negative-result source and don't put failed VCT in the final claimed contribution.
issues.status: Strength; no adverse correction beyond synchronization

issues.claim: ESA exceeds the original paper's best of ten methods in the balanced IID setting.
issues.evidence: The numbers are promising: MNIST 97.62 vs 96.44; CIFAR10 60.93 vs 59.36; SVHN 77.07 vs 76.26; FashionMNIST Ours-A 83.96 slightly below 84.28, MC-B 85.75 above. However `best_mean_acc` selects best round by test accuracy and the comparisons span published paper results vs own runs with some reproduction deltas. Different variants (Ours-A vs Ours-A-B) must not be blended into the same claim.
issues.impact: The balanced comparison is useful but weak as a confirmatory result, particularly small margins and variant selection.
issues.author_counterargument: The paper reproduces original protocol and acknowledges small balanced gains, frozen FE differences and the best-of-ten baseline.
issues.resolution: Use validation checkpoint selection for new results, clearly mark historical replication metric, compare same version on same splits, and label MC-B separately with its seed uncertainty.

issues.claim: The paper's classifier-side balanced-bias calibration is adequately distinguished from the current prior art.
issues.evidence: The current related-work draft (identified as searched 2026-10-09) discusses CCVR, CReFF and Fed3R but does not mention FedNPC, published in CVPR Findings 2026. FedNPC explicitly studies post-hoc classifier calibration for federated long-tailed learning using a virtual balanced dataset. ESA's BBC calibrates predictions using balanced anchored synthetic features, so this is a close method to compare. Primary source: https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2026F/html/Gao_FedNPC_Stochastic_Noise-driven_Post-hoc_Classifier_Calibration_Method_for_Federated_Long-tailed_CVPRF_2026_paper.html.
issues.impact: A current and close calibration paper is missing from novelty framing; depending on protocol/assumptions, it may reduce the apparent originality of BBC and may be a necessary baseline. This does not negate the separate generator-anchoring contribution.
issues.author_counterargument: FedNPC is not necessarily designed for generator-based heterogeneous heads or uses the same feature-space/communication assumptions; methodological differences may remain substantial.
issues.resolution: Read and cite FedNPC's primary paper; compare objective, calibration data/statistics, assumptions, privacy, and compatibility with heterogeneous private heads. Include a matched baseline if it fits the setting, or clearly explain the incompatibility.
issues.status: New likely omission; must verify fit and compare
